title: Count Atoms by Weighing? Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
A dozen is twelve eggs and a ream is five hundred sheets: counting words make big numbers easy. Atoms are far too many to count one by one, so chemists count them the way a shop counts tiny steel balls, by weighing. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 1, Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry) we meet the chemist's dozen: the mole.

On the molecule bench, carbon-12 atoms pour onto a scale while a live counter climbs. One atom weighs 1.992648 × 10^-23 g; at exactly 12 g the counter stops at 6.022 × 10^23, the Avogadro constant NA. Step by step we derive it, and see why 1 u × NA = 1 g, so a particle of x u makes a mole of x grams. One mole of hydrogen atoms and one mole of water sit on one balance (with a pause and think check), then molar mass in g mol^-1 (water 18.02, sodium chloride 58.5). A worked example counts the molecules in a 9 g sip of water (3.011 × 10^23), then the atoms vs molecules exam trap, an original NEET pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 9 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students.
